draft.title: How quotations can be repurposed
card: A quotation is words taken from a longer text. When it is cut out, the words around it are lost.
Those lost words can change the meaning. A writer can leave out a "but" or a joke, so the quotation says something the speaker did not mean.
Example: a coach says the team played badly in the first half, but fought back to win. A headline that quotes only "played badly" gives a different message.
To check a quotation, find the original source. Ask who said it, when and why, and what came just before and after.
draft.remember: A quotation can change meaning when its context is cut away, so find the original.

a.q: Why can a quotation mislead a reader?
opts: Cutting it out removes the words that shaped its meaning
Quotations always contain facts that are not true
Quotations are written by people who want to deceive
Short quotations are always harder to understand
a.why: The words before and after a quotation can change what it means. Taking it out removes them. Quotations are not always false or deceptive: many are accurate, and the problem is the missing context.
a.clue: Think about what is left behind when words are cut out.

b.q: Ravi tells a reporter he found the new bus timetable confusing at first, but now likes it. A poster quotes him saying only "confusing at first". What is the best way to check this poster?
opts: Find the full interview to see what Ravi said around it
Count how many words are in the quotation on the poster
Ask whether the poster uses quotation marks correctly
Check whether the poster has a picture of Ravi on it
b.why: The full interview shows that Ravi went on to say he liked the timetable, so the poster changes his view. Correct quotation marks do not prove the words are used fairly, because the missing part is the problem.
b.clue: What would show the words that were left out?

a.best: Cutting it out removes the words that shaped its meaning

b.best: Find the full interview to see what Ravi said around it
